newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico PRI to consider expelling Carlos Salinas.
newsitem.headline: Mexico PRI to consider expelling Carlos Salinas.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) will meet this week to reconsider a proposal to expel disgraced former president Carlos Salinas de Gortari from the party, a top PRI official said on Tuesday.
"In the next few days in this week the Honour and Justice Commission of the party will take a decision and clear up this matter," PRI Secretary-General Juan S. Millan told reporters.
Millan refused to say whether he would support requests from rank-and-file members to expel Salinas, saying only that the party would respect the commission's decision.
Carlos Salinas won huge acclaim during his 1988-94 presidency but fell into disgrace almost immediately afterward as the economy collapsed, the peso plummeted and accusations of corruption mounted.

Following demands from PRI militants, the party decided in January 1996 to expel Carlos's brother Raul -- imprisoned since 1995 on murder and illicit enrichment charges -- but did not decide the former president's fate.

PRI president Humberto Roque Villanueva told Reuters in an interview two weeks ago that the party would expel Carlos Salinas if it were proven he had broken the law. Roque said he had yet to see conclusive evidence that this was the case.

But the PRI leader said on Friday his party was "politically and morally distanced" from Salinas and accused the former president of being ideologically closer to the conservative opposition party PAN than to the PRI.
Like other party figures, Millan has blamed the Salinas brothers for the PRI's poor image and recent electoral losses.
Political analysts say the PRI faces a tricky choice if it decides to throw Salinas out and repudiate his legacy.

Zedillo's economic programme is very similar to Salinas's and many participants in the previous government are still in power under Zedillo, making it difficult to credibly disassociate the PRI from Salinas.
This led one cartoonist to comment sarcastically last week that "all the PRI now needs to do is to distance itself from the PRI" in order to win voters over.
